description:
We are a multidisciplinary team of 6 students from UPSRJ driven by building innovative, interactive solutions. Our skills span Python, C# (Unity), AI tools, data analytics, and hardware integration with Arduino, all combined with creative design. We aim to transform complex NASA challenges into polished, practical, and engaging solutions while pushing our technical boundaries together.

God bless you all :)
summary:
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 – Space Mission Design Game

Our project is a responsible, educational, and cooperative web-based video game designed for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026. Playable directly in a web browser and optimized for mobile devices, it supports 1–4 players in approximately 5-minute sessions.

Players become space engineers working together to design and operate a spacecraft through eight interactive minigames and a spaceflight simulation.

The game features three missions inspired by NASA: a Moon roundtrip, near-Earth asteroid exploration, and a Mars sample return mission. Players manage budgets, launch vehicles, spacecraft mass, orbital mechanics, energy, scientific instruments, and communications. Every decision is interconnected through real physics equations and engineering principles.

Teams must collaborate, solve challenges, manage resources, and respond to unexpected spaceflight emergencies. At the end, a mission report evaluates their performance and explains the consequences of their decisions.

Technology: React, TypeScript, FastAPI, Socket.IO, and Three.js.

Goal: Make space engineering accessible and engaging while promoting scientific literacy, teamwork, critical thinking, and responsible learning through an interactive web experience.
details:
What does it do and how does it work? Astro Squad is a 100% web-based, 5-minute cooperative space mission design game for 1 to 4 players (Singleplayer or Kahoot-style PIN Multiplayer, with an adaptive AI synthesizer filling empty seats). Players choose one of three NASA-inspired missions (Operation Artemis: Lunar Return, Near-Earth Asteroid Hunter, or Mars Sample Return & MRO Orbiter) and divide into four specialized roles: Finance & Launch, Spacecraft & Mass, Orbit & Power, and Science & Comms. Crewmates advance automatically along a two-wave linear track of 8 interactive 2D/3D minigames—covering UFE budget allocation, topological spacecraft assembly, Tsiolkovsky orbital propulsion, spectral lab calibration, rocket/rideshare selection, 2D Center of Gravity balancing, Three.js 3D rover power harvesting, and DSN antenna tracking/DTMF filtering—where every decision mutates teammates' physical constraints in real time and updates a live 4-gate launch forecast. At liftoff, the crew enters a 60 Seconds!-inspired 4-chapter cabin survival flight with turn-based crisis logbook decisions and random space hazards, ending with a causal NASA feedback report, a 0–1,000 score, a crew collaboration leaderboard, and an instant Redesign & Retry loop.

What benefits does it have? Astro Squad runs directly in any desktop or mobile browser with zero downloads, accounts, or specialized hardware, and includes an instant English/Spanish language switch plus an automatic offline preview fallback. Instead of memorizing isolated equations, players see firsthand how a single trade-off—such as adding a heavier instrument or cutting R&D funding—ripples across total wet mass, budget, power, propellant requirements, Center of Gravity, and Deep Space Network (DSN) downlink hours. Built-in station briefings, plain-language flight logbooks, and step-by-step spectral guides make orbital mechanics and aerospace systems engineering approachable with no prior background required.

What is the intended impact of the project? Our goal is to bridge the gap between theoretical STEM exercises and how real NASA concurrent engineering teams negotiate mission trade-offs under pressure. Designed for classrooms, STEM workshops, and public outreach, Astro Squad lets students collaborate from their own phones in 4-person squads while comparing scores across iterations. By turning mission failure into a clear, numerical diagnostic tool rather than a dead end, the game builds lasting intuition around financial safety reserves (NPR 7120.5 UFE), mass growth margins (JPL CML 4), communications bottlenecks, and iterative engineering design.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, and software did we use? The frontend is built with TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, Three.js, tsParticles, Lucide React, Socket.IO Client, and a procedural Web Audio API synthesizer (SoundEngine.tsx). The backend runs on Python 3.12 with FastAPI, Uvicorn, python-socketio, Pydantic v2, NumPy, SciPy, and Pytest, integrating a custom FTIR/NIST spectral analysis engine (logica/ and juegos_espectrales/). Supporting workflows include Node.js monorepo scripts, a Python Pillow/NumPy/SciPy sprite-processing pipeline, standard team laptops and smartphones (100% software, no custom hardware), and cloud deployment via Netlify (frontend) and Render (backend). In accordance with Space Apps guidelines, we disclose that AI assistants supported code, test, and translation authoring under human verification, and AI-generated sprite sheets and nebula backgrounds carry visible "AI-generated art" watermarks.

How is your project creative? Rather than building a dry spreadsheet simulator, we fused a Paper Mario × Flash Arcade art direction and a 60 Seconds! spacecraft cabin diorama with a NASA telemetry HUD and four original vector specialists (ASTRO_ENGINEER, ASTRO_MEDIC, ASTRO_SOLDIER, ASTRO_DEFENDER). We transformed real spectroscopy—Wien's law, Balmer lines, FTIR mineral bands, Cauchy optical dispersion, and ITU-T Q.23 DTMF interference filtering—into tactile Science and Comms puzzles, paired with procedural zero-file Web Audio SFX. Most uniquely, teammates' live controls asymmetrically reshape one another's gameplay in real time: Finance's R&D factor dynamically shifts Hydrogen Fuel Cell spawn rates inside Orbit's 3D rover arena, while Science's selected instruments physically drop onto Mass Balance's Center of Gravity grid.

What factors did our team consider? Scientific validity came first: all constants, orbits, launchers, and instruments live in a unified catalog (nasa_catalog.json) citing WGS84, NIST, JPL DESCANSO (MRO), LRO, OSIRIS-REx, Artemis I/II, ITU-R P.525, and SpaceX Rideshare v11, while explicitly labeling game-scaled estimates. To coordinate a 5-person team across 24 hours, we enforced strict TypeScript/Pydantic interface contracts (MinigameProps), an isolated /dev-sandbox, server-authoritative physics with liftoff state snapshots, and automated Pytest verification. Finally, we designed for real-world resilience and compliance by proxying WebSockets for LAN/cloud play, supporting 375 px mobile screens with color-plus-icon accessibility, excluding all NASA logos and copyrighted silhouettes, and visibly watermarking AI-generated art.
